section.title: Advanced Directus
section.description: Seventeen focused lessons: five API and automation labs, plus twelve UI/UX component and chart labs. Each lesson ends with a hands-on lab that runs against a real Directus instance.

lessons.title: Flows: the mental model
lessons.outcome: Read any Directus Flow as a trigger, a chain of operations, and one data object moving through them.
mental_model: **Trigger** decides when the Flow runs. Event hooks watch data, webhooks watch HTTP, schedules watch the clock.
**Operations** decide what happens. Each one reads the data chain and writes its result under its key.
**$trigger, $last, and $env** are your handles. A Filter (blocking) trigger can rewrite a payload before it is saved.

lab.title: Enrich a note with a blocking Flow
lab.instructions: Create a note. A Filter Flow runs before the insert and adds slug, word_count, and source. Change the title and run it again to see the derived fields update.
lab.expected:
{
  "id": "…",
  "title": "Hello Flows",
  "body": "Directus flows can enrich a record before it is saved.",
  "slug": "hello-flows",
  "word_count": 10,
  "source": "flow",
  "status": "draft"
}
hints: The Flow is attached to the lab_notes collection.
A Filter trigger runs before the database insert.
If you change the title, the slug changes with it.

lessons.takeaway: A blocking Flow is middleware for your data: it can validate, transform, or cancel the write.

knowledge_check.question: Which trigger type can change a payload before it is written?
knowledge_check.explanation: A Filter (blocking) event hook pauses the transaction, lets the Flow transform the payload, and then resumes the write.

deep_dive.title: The five trigger types
deep_dive.body: Event hook, webhook, schedule (CRON), another Flow, and manual. Most automations start with an event hook or a webhook.

deep_dive.title: Blocking vs non-blocking
deep_dive.body: Filter hooks block the transaction and can cancel it. Action hooks run after the commit and are better for notifications and slow side effects.

deep_dive.title: The data chain
deep_dive.body: Every Flow starts with $trigger, $accountability, $env, and $last. Each operation appends its output under its own key.

lessons.title: Webhooks and third-party calls
lessons.outcome: Expose a Flow as an HTTP endpoint, call an external service, and return the result to the caller.
mental_model: A **webhook trigger** is just a URL: POST /flows/trigger/:id.
Turn **Asynchronous** off and set **Response Body** to return the Flow result synchronously.
The **Request URL** operation handles method, headers, and body. Keep secrets in env vars and design for retries.

lab.title: Call a weather service through a Flow
lab.instructions: Send a city to the webhook Flow. The Flow calls the local mock weather API and returns a normalized forecast. Try Manila, Tokyo, or Oslo.
hints: The webhook receives the JSON body as $trigger.
The Flow calls the mock API with the city and units.
Response Body is set to the last operation, so the HTTP response is the forecast.

lessons.takeaway: A synchronous webhook Flow is a small integration endpoint you can build without deploying a new service.

knowledge_check.question: Why should a webhook receiver be idempotent?
options: So retries do not create duplicate side effects
So Directus can cache the response
So the payload can be larger
knowledge_check.explanation: Networks retry. An idempotent receiver detects a repeated event and avoids charging, shipping, or creating the same thing twice.

deep_dive.title: Webhook vs event hook
deep_dive.body: Event hooks start inside Directus when data changes. Webhooks start outside Directus when an HTTP request arrives. Both can run the same operations.

deep_dive.title: Secrets and headers
deep_dive.body: The lab Flow sends an x-lab-secret header from an environment variable. Never hard-code API keys in a Flow or in browser code.

deep_dive.title: Retries and idempotency
deep_dive.body: Use a stable event ID, store processed IDs, and make the receiver safe to call more than once. Log failures so a retry can be replayed.

lessons.title: Extending Directus
lessons.outcome: Choose the right extension type, call a custom endpoint, and recognize when configuration is enough.
mental_model: **App extensions** change the Studio: interface, display, layout, module, panel, theme.
**API extensions** change the server: endpoint, hook, operation.
Build only when configuration cannot do it. Every extension is code you own and must maintain.

lab.title: Call a custom endpoint
lab.instructions: This project ships a tiny endpoint extension at /labs-endpoint. Call it and inspect the response. Then edit the interface config below to see how a custom field control is shaped.
hints: The extension is mounted under its package name.
Custom endpoints are normal Express routes.
The response includes the extension name.

interfacePreview.title: Rating interface
interfacePreview.description: A custom interface receives a value and options, then emits a new value. Edit the config and try the control.

lessons.takeaway: Extensions are how Directus stays small: add the behavior you need without forking the core.

knowledge_check.question: Which extension type adds a new top-level page to the Studio?
knowledge_check.explanation: A module adds a top-level entry to the Studio navigation. Interfaces and displays affect fields; endpoints add API routes.

deep_dive.title: Extension types
deep_dive.body: App: interface, display, layout, module, panel, theme. API: endpoint, hook, operation. Bundles combine several types into one package.

deep_dive.title: Anatomy of an endpoint
deep_dive.body: The default export receives an Express router. Routes mount under the extension name. Use Directus services from context when you need permissions or database access.

deep_dive.title: When not to build
deep_dive.body: Try a Flow, a preset, a field option, or a built-in interface first. Extensions are powerful, but they are also long-lived maintenance.

lessons.title: Real-time with WebSockets
lessons.outcome: Subscribe to a collection and handle create, update, and delete events as they happen.
mental_model: A **WebSocket** stays open; subscriptions push changes instead of polling.
Authenticate first, then subscribe with a collection, event filter, and field list.
Handle **ping** with **pong**, and use Redis pub/sub when you run more than one Directus instance.

lab.title: Watch a record arrive live
lab.instructions: Open a subscription to lab_notes, then create a note. The create event should arrive in the console without a page refresh. This demo uses Directus public WebSocket mode, so it can only see the public lab_notes read permission.
hints: Subscribe before creating the note.
The confirmation event is subscription with event init.
The create event contains only the fields you requested.

lessons.takeaway: Use WebSockets for live dashboards and collaborative screens; keep REST for normal reads and writes.

knowledge_check.question: What event confirms that a subscription is active?
knowledge_check.explanation: Directus replies with a subscription message and event: init as soon as the subscription is registered.

deep_dive.title: The subscribe message
deep_dive.body: Send type: subscribe, a collection, an optional event filter, and an optional fields query. The server sends create, update, and delete events.

deep_dive.title: Authentication
deep_dive.body: Send an auth message with a valid access token before subscribing. Public read permissions can make a demo public, but production data should be scoped.

deep_dive.title: Scaling
deep_dive.body: One Directus instance can hold the connection. With multiple instances, use Redis pub/sub so every instance broadcasts to its own clients.

lessons.title: Capstone: order automation
lessons.outcome: Combine a trigger, validation, an external call, a write-back, and a response in one Flow.
mental_model: Design the **data chain** first: what each operation receives and returns.
Validate early and fail loudly. Keep external calls idempotent.
Write the result back to Directus so the automation is observable.

lab.title: Run the order Flow
lab.instructions: Send an order to the capstone webhook. The Flow validates it, applies a tier discount, calls mock shipping, saves a note, and returns a summary. Try a total of 0 to see the validation failure.
hints: gold gets 15%, silver 10%, bronze 5%.
Try total: 0 to see the Flow reject the order.
Find the saved note in Directus under lab_notes.

lessons.takeaway: Production automation is a chain of small, observable steps — not one giant script.

knowledge_check.question: What should happen when the shipping API times out?
options: Retry safely, using an idempotency key
knowledge_check.explanation: Retries are normal. A stable idempotency key lets the receiver detect the duplicate and return the original result instead of creating a second shipment.

deep_dive.title: Failure branches
deep_dive.body: Give each external call a reject path. Log the input, the response, and the error so a failed run can be replayed.

deep_dive.title: Idempotency
deep_dive.body: Use the order ID as the idempotency key. Store it before calling the external service, and check it before doing the side effect.

deep_dive.title: Observability
deep_dive.body: Write a record back to Directus, add a status field, and keep the Flow log. If something fails at 2 a.m., you want a trail.

lessons.title: Build a button
lessons.outcome: Create a primary button with clear states, a comfortable hit area, and a visible keyboard focus.
mental_model: **States are part of the component.** Default, hover, active, focus-visible, and disabled each tell the user something.
**Affordance beats decoration.** A button should look pressable and clearly name the action.
**Accessibility is design.** Contrast, a 44px target, and a focus ring make the button usable by everyone.

lab.title: Style the primary button
lab.brief: Start with a plain button. Add the states and make it feel like one component, not five one-off styles.

solution.html:
<main class="button-demo">
  <button class="button" type="button">Save changes</button>
  <button class="button" type="button" disabled>Disabled</button>
</main>

hints: Use :focus-visible, not just :focus.
A 44px minimum height is a good mobile target.
Disabled styles still need readable text.

lessons.takeaway: A button is a small state machine: every state should look intentional and remain accessible.

knowledge_check.question: Which state is essential for keyboard users but often forgotten?
knowledge_check.explanation: focus-visible shows a clear ring when the button is reached with the keyboard, without showing it for every mouse click.

deep_dive.title: Contrast
deep_dive.body: Text needs roughly 4.5:1 contrast; interactive boundaries and focus indicators need roughly 3:1. Test the disabled state too, even though disabled text has more leeway.

deep_dive.title: Hit area
deep_dive.body: A 44x44px target is comfortable on touch screens. Padding is usually a better way to reach it than increasing font size.

deep_dive.title: Loading and disabled
deep_dive.body: Disabled prevents action; loading explains why action is temporarily unavailable. Do not use one as a substitute for the other.

lessons.title: Build a form
lessons.outcome: Create a semantic form with labeled fields, sensible input types, and a clear success state.
mental_model: **Labels are part of the input.** A placeholder is not a label.
**Use the right input type.** Email, text, and textarea change the keyboard and validation behavior.
**Feedback closes the loop.** The form should say what happened after submit.

lab.title: Build a contact form
lab.brief: Build a name, email, and message form. Validate on submit and show a success message instead of reloading the page.

solution.html:

hints: Connect each label with for and id.
Use autocomplete=name and autocomplete=email.
role=status announces the success message.

lessons.takeaway: A form is a conversation: labels ask, input types guide, and status messages answer.

knowledge_check.question: Which attributes connect a label to an input?
knowledge_check.explanation: The label's for attribute must match the input's id. Clicking the label then focuses the input, and screen readers announce them together.

deep_dive.title: Labels vs placeholders
deep_dive.body: A placeholder disappears after typing and is not a reliable label. Keep a visible label above the field and use the placeholder for an example.

deep_dive.title: Validation
deep_dive.body: Use the right input type and required attribute first. Add custom messages only when the native behavior is not clear enough.

deep_dive.title: Accessible status
deep_dive.body: role=status announces a polite update like “Message sent.” Move focus only when the next action requires it.

lessons.title: Design a form
lessons.outcome: Finish a designed form with visible focus, clear status feedback, and a layout that holds up on small screens.
mental_model: **States are part of the design.** Focus, success, and error should be visible, not implied.
**Spacing is structure.** Group related fields and give the submit action room.
**Feedback is visual and textual.** Color alone does not explain an error.

lab.title: Design the form states
lab.brief: This form already uses the Directus card style. Finish the interaction design: add Directus focus rings, a status that uses text and color, and a single-column layout below 560px.
checklist: Branded focus ring on every control
Labels stay visible above each field

solution.html:

hints: Use :focus-visible with #6644ff.
Set status.dataset.state before writing the message.
Add one media query at 560px; keep the card padding comfortable.

lessons.takeaway: A designed form stays clear when it is focused, invalid, or narrow.

knowledge_check.question: Besides turning red, what should an error message do?
options: Explain what to fix and tie to the field
knowledge_check.explanation: An error should say what went wrong, how to fix it, and be associated with the field so it is announced and easy to find.

deep_dive.title: 8-point spacing
deep_dive.body: Use a small scale such as 8, 16, 24, 32. Consistent spacing creates hierarchy without adding borders or decoration.

deep_dive.title: Error placement
deep_dive.body: Place the message next to the field it belongs to, mark the field with aria-invalid, and keep the original label visible.

deep_dive.title: Responsive forms
deep_dive.body: A single-column form is usually the best mobile layout. Keep the submit action full width and the focus ring visible.

lessons.title: Build a relational item picker
lessons.outcome: Design a Directus relational picker that exposes collection context, selected records, and a clear way to change the relationship.
mental_model: **Relationships are content context.** A picker should tell editors which collection they are choosing from before showing the selected item.
**Selection is state.** Empty, selected, loading, and invalid states need different labels and actions.
**The interface should stay reversible.** Clear and change actions are safer than forcing an editor to reopen the entire form.

lab.title: Build a relational item picker
lab.brief: Create a picker surface for a Directus article relationship. Make the current selection obvious, show collection context, and keep the open and clear actions usable by keyboard.
checklist: Selected item has a readable name
Change and clear actions have names
The picker remains usable on a narrow screen

hints: Start with the selected record, then design the empty state.
Use a collection label such as Articles or Authors.
Keep the clear action separate from the primary picker action.

lessons.takeaway: Design a Directus relational picker that exposes collection context, selected records, and a clear way to change the relationship.

knowledge_check.question: What makes this CMS-specific?
options: Use the CMS-supported field behavior and its real state
Hide all state from the editor
knowledge_check.explanation: The component should reflect the CMS feature and preserve clear, editable state.

deep_dive.title: State is part of the schema
deep_dive.body: A useful admin component reflects the data shape and the CMS state instead of hiding important context behind decoration.

deep_dive.title: Responsive editing
deep_dive.body: Admin interfaces should keep labels and actions reachable when the viewport becomes narrow.

deep_dive.title: Accessible controls
deep_dive.body: Use labels, focus styles, and text alternatives so the component remains understandable without color or hover.

lessons.title: Design a permission-aware state
lessons.outcome: Create a Directus interface that explains why an editor can view, edit, or not access a field without exposing confusing controls.
mental_model: **Access is part of the UI.** A disabled control without a reason makes an access rule feel like a broken interface.
**View and edit are different capabilities.** Show readable content even when mutation is unavailable.
**Explain the next step.** Restricted states should name the permission or role path when possible.

lab.title: Design a permission-aware state
lab.brief: Build a permission-aware field card with view, edit, and restricted states. Use copy and affordances that make Directus access rules understandable.
checklist: Edit action appears only when allowed
Status is not conveyed by color alone

field access

hints: Compare an editor role with a read-only role.
Use a lock icon only as support for text.
Do not show a fake save button in the restricted state.

lessons.takeaway: Create a Directus interface that explains why an editor can view, edit, or not access a field without exposing confusing controls.

knowledge_check.question: What makes this CMS-specific?
options: Use the CMS-supported field behavior and its real state
Hide all state from the editor

deep_dive.body: Admin interfaces should keep labels and actions reachable when the viewport becomes narrow.

deep_dive.title: Accessible controls
deep_dive.body: Use labels, focus styles, and text alternatives so the component remains understandable without color or hover.

lessons.title: Build a Flow run status panel
lessons.outcome: Design a Directus Flow status panel that separates running, succeeded, and failed automation states with useful recovery actions.
mental_model: **Automation needs feedback.** A trigger that ran successfully should say what happened, not only show a spinner.
**Failure is actionable.** Include a retry or inspect action and keep the error close to the failed step.
**Status has a lifecycle.** Running, success, and failure should not share one ambiguous message.

lab.title: Build a Flow run status panel
lab.brief: Compose a status panel for an order-enrichment Flow. Make the current run state, timestamp, and recovery action readable at a glance.
checklist: The last run time is visible
Status text does not rely on color
The panel remains useful without live updates

lessons.takeaway: Design a Directus Flow status panel that separates running, succeeded, and failed automation states with useful recovery actions.

lessons.title: Build a numeric data table
lessons.outcome: Create a small table of numbers, style it with the shared build controls, save it to Directus, and read the same rows in the Level 8 chart.
mental_model: **The form is the schema.** Title, caption, unit, and rows are the data contract the chart reads.
**Reuse the controls.** The same BuilderFields inputs and design tokens drive the form and the live table.
**Save, then fetch.** The table is stored in the CMS; Level 8 loads the newest saved table and turns it into a bar chart.
**Keep it small.** A short numeric table is easy to validate, reload, and chart.

lab.title: Save a table of numbers
lab.brief: Edit the rows and labels, adjust the design tokens, then save the table to Directus. The newest saved table becomes the saved-form chart in the Level 8 showcase.
checklist: Every row has a label and a number
The table title describes the data
The design tokens still pass contrast
The table is saved in the CMS

content.title: Daily active learners
content.caption: Two weeks of daily learners saved in Directus and reused by the Level 8 chart.

hints: Use the Number rows list to add, remove, or reorder rows.
The chart uses the row labels as categories and the values as bars.
Save again to update the same table, or reset to start a new version.

lessons.takeaway: A small, validated table saved in Directus is enough data to drive a real chart without exposing the CMS credentials.

knowledge_check.question: Where should the Level 8 chart get the numbers from the form?
options: From the newest saved data-table component in Directus
From a hard-coded array in the chart component
From the browser's local storage only
knowledge_check.explanation: The form saves its rows in Directus. The Level 8 server loader reads the newest saved table, validates the rows, and passes a small chart-ready series to the browser.

deep_dive.title: Why store rows, not markup?
deep_dive.body: The builder saves the labels and numbers as structured content. The preview can change without losing the data, and the chart reads the same values instead of scraping the table.

deep_dive.title: One contract, two views
deep_dive.body: The form preview and the Level 8 chart both consume the same title, unit, and row objects. That keeps the data honest when either view changes.

deep_dive.title: Small data is still data
deep_dive.body: Validation belongs at the edge: require labels, finite numbers, and a bounded row count so a malformed table cannot break the chart.

lessons.title: Build a dashboard card
lessons.outcome: Compose a responsive dashboard card that makes the metric, trend, and next action easy to scan.
mental_model: **Hierarchy creates speed.** A useful card answers what changed before it explains why.
**Responsive is a content decision.** Let the metric stay prominent while supporting details adapt to the available width.
**Actions need context.** A link or button should name the destination instead of relying on an icon alone.

lab.title: Compose a dashboard card
lab.brief: Turn the starter metric into a responsive card. Keep the primary number prominent, show the trend in text and color, and make the details link keyboard accessible.
checklist: Metric has a clear label and unit
Trend is explained with text, not color alone
Details action has an accessible name
Focus ring is visible on the action

hints: Use a heading for the metric and keep the number visually prominent.
Pair trend color with an arrow and words such as “this month.”
Test the preview at a narrow width, not just at desktop size.

lessons.takeaway: A dashboard card is successful when someone can scan the metric, its meaning, and the next action in one pass.

knowledge_check.question: What makes a positive trend accessible?
options: Text and a visual treatment that reinforce each other
knowledge_check.explanation: Color and icons can be missed or misunderstood. The trend should also be stated in words so its meaning is available to everyone.

deep_dive.title: Scan order
deep_dive.body: Lead with the label and number, then provide the trend and details. Avoid making a decorative chart compete with the metric.

deep_dive.title: Responsive composition
deep_dive.body: A card can change from two columns to a vertical stack without changing the information hierarchy.

deep_dive.title: Action labels
deep_dive.body: “View publishing details” is more useful to screen readers and keyboard users than an unlabeled arrow icon.

lessons.title: Build an accessible dialog
lessons.outcome: Create a dialog that has a clear escape route, a labelled title, and predictable keyboard behavior.
mental_model: **A dialog interrupts the page.** Explain why it opened and offer a clear way to leave.
**Focus must have a home.** Move focus into the dialog and return it to the trigger when the dialog closes.
**Danger deserves friction.** Destructive actions should be explicit and visually distinct from cancel.

lab.title: Design a delete confirmation
lab.brief: Complete the delete confirmation dialog. Make the trigger open it, support Escape and the cancel action, and announce the dialog title and destructive action clearly.

starter.html:
Delete this draft?

This action cannot be undone.

solution.html:
Delete this draft?

This action cannot be undone. The draft will be removed permanently.

hints: Use role=dialog, aria-modal, and labelledby/describedby together.
Store the trigger before opening so focus can return there.
Escape should close the dialog without confirming the destructive action.

lessons.takeaway: A dialog is an interaction contract: label it, contain the interruption, and always provide a safe way back.

knowledge_check.question: Where should focus go after a dialog closes?
options: The element that opened the dialog
The first heading in the page
knowledge_check.explanation: Returning focus to the trigger preserves the user's place and prevents keyboard users from losing context.

deep_dive.title: Dialog semantics
deep_dive.body: A labelled dialog gives assistive technology a useful announcement. aria-describedby adds the consequence or supporting context.

deep_dive.title: Focus containment
deep_dive.body: A production dialog should keep Tab inside the modal while it is open. The lab starts with Escape and focus restoration as the essential foundation.

deep_dive.title: Destructive actions
deep_dive.body: Use a specific action label such as “Delete draft,” not a vague “OK,” so the consequence is clear before activation.

lessons.title: Design loading and empty states
lessons.outcome: Turn waiting and no-results moments into useful UI with honest status, next steps, and accessible announcements.
mental_model: **Empty is not broken.** Explain why there is no content and what the user can do next.
**Loading sets expectations.** Show progress without pretending data has arrived.
**Status needs a channel.** Use text and live-region semantics so updates are available beyond sight.

lab.title: Complete the collection states
lab.brief: Design a collection panel that can explain loading and no results. Add an accessible status message and a useful next action without relying on a spinner alone.
checklist: Empty state explains the next step
No state relies on color alone

hints: A loading message explains what is happening; a spinner alone does not.
Use role=status with aria-live=polite for non-urgent updates.
Keep the empty-state action specific to the next useful step.

lessons.takeaway: Loading and empty states are part of the product experience: they reduce uncertainty and give the user a clear next move.

knowledge_check.question: What should an empty state include?
options: An explanation and a useful next action
A red error message every time
knowledge_check.explanation: An empty state should explain the situation and help the user recover or make progress.

deep_dive.title: Loading versus error
deep_dive.body: Loading means the request is still in progress. Error means the request failed. Do not use the same message for both states.

deep_dive.title: Live regions
deep_dive.body: role=status and aria-live=polite let assistive technology announce a changing status without interrupting the user's current task.

deep_dive.title: Useful emptiness
deep_dive.body: The best empty state is specific to the collection. “Create article” is more actionable than “Nothing here.”

lessons.title: Build a responsive bar chart
lessons.outcome: Design a responsive Directus bar chart that lets readers compare editorial activity while keeping labels and values easy to scan.
mental_model: **Compare before decorating.** A bar earns its space by making category differences immediate.
**The row is the contract.** Labels, values, and units stay editable so the chart is never disconnected from CMS content.
**Responsive is a reading order.** Keep labels, values, and the strongest comparison available as the card narrows.

lab.title: Compare editorial activity
lab.brief: Enter category values from your Directus workflow and tune the card styling. The bars resize with the container and update as you edit each number.
checklist: Bar lengths reflect the edited values
The highest value is still readable on mobile
The unit is visible beside the chart
The customized chart data is saved in Directus

content.title: Stories by channel
content.caption: Compare where this week’s published stories came from.

hints: Keep category labels short so each bar has room on narrow screens.
Change one category at a time and check whether the ranking still tells the intended story.
Use a consistent unit so the bar lengths are not misread.

lessons.takeaway: A bar chart is strongest when Directus categories are comparable, ordered intentionally, and still legible when the layout narrows.

knowledge_check.question: Which change should immediately alter a bar chart?
knowledge_check.explanation: The bars are derived from the structured row values, so changing a value changes its bar length.

deep_dive.title: Comparison first
deep_dive.body: Bars support side-by-side comparison when categories share a unit. Sort or order them intentionally instead of letting the visual order happen by accident.

deep_dive.title: Mobile hierarchy
deep_dive.body: On a narrow screen, preserve the title, unit, and relative bar lengths. Short labels and a bounded row count prevent the chart from becoming a horizontal scroll problem.

deep_dive.title: CMS contract
deep_dive.body: The chart consumes structured rows rather than rendered markup, so the same saved CMS values can support another visual treatment later.

lessons.title: Build a responsive line chart
lessons.outcome: Create a responsive Directus line chart that explains change over time instead of treating a sequence of values as unrelated cards.
mental_model: **Sequence creates meaning.** A line connects ordered observations, so the labels must describe a real progression.
**Points need context.** The line shows shape, while endpoint values and units keep the insight precise.
**Responsive is not smaller desktop.** The chart can resize while the summary and labels preserve the message.

lab.title: Trace a publishing trend
lab.brief: Shape a time-ordered Directus series, choose a clear accent, and test how the line and points behave when values and labels change.
checklist: Labels follow a meaningful time order
The line makes direction easy to see
Points remain visible at narrow widths
The first and latest values are summarized
The customized trend data is saved in Directus

content.title: Daily publishing pace
content.caption: A seven-day sequence for spotting momentum and dips.

hints: Keep rows in chronological order so the line has a truthful direction.
Test a sharp dip and a recovery to see whether the story remains understandable.
Use the endpoint summary as a text alternative to visual inspection.

lessons.takeaway: A line chart gives Directus time-series data a reading order: the sequence and endpoint context matter as much as the styling.

knowledge_check.question: What makes a line chart meaningful?
options: An ordered sequence with a clear unit
knowledge_check.explanation: A line implies continuity, so its rows need an intentional order and a clear measurement.

deep_dive.title: Ordered observations
deep_dive.body: A line suggests continuity. Use it for a meaningful sequence and avoid implying a trend when the categories have no natural order.

deep_dive.title: Accessible summary
deep_dive.body: Keep endpoint values and units in text so the insight survives without pointer hover, fine-grained SVG inspection, or color perception.

deep_dive.title: Responsive points
deep_dive.body: A responsive chart changes its available width, not the underlying data. The normalized rows remain the source of truth.
